title: Stateless Services
subtitle: Watch a login break when a request reaches the wrong server, then see how moving session data out of the servers fixes it.
learn: What state a server holds between requests and why that blocks scaling
Why round-robin load balancing logs users out of stateful servers
How sticky sessions work and what they cost you
Two ways to go stateless: a shared session store and signed tokens
Why stateless servers can be added, removed or killed freely

steps.title: Why did my login vanish?
steps.body: You log in to a shop and fill your cart. A minute later you see the login page again and your cart is empty. Your password was fine. What happened is that a different server answered, or the server that knew you was replaced. This lesson is about what that server was remembering, and where it should have kept it instead.
steps.idea: If your login only works on the one server that handled it, scaling out and server failures both break it.
steps.caption: The request reaches a server that does not know you.

steps.title: State lives in server memory
steps.body: HTTP forgets you between requests, so apps use a session: a small record such as "user 42, cart with 3 items", stored under a random ID. Here you log in and the request lands on server A. A keeps the session in its own memory and sends back the ID as a cookie (a small value your browser attaches to every later request). The browser holds only the ID, not the data. A now holds data that the next request depends on, so A is called stateful.
steps.idea: A stateful server remembers something between requests that no other server knows.
steps.caption: Login lands on A, so the session exists only in A's memory.

steps.title: Round robin hits the wrong server
steps.body: Your next click goes to server B, because the load balancer is taking turns (round robin). B receives your cookie sid=9f2 but has never seen that ID, so it treats you as logged out and replies 401. With two servers about half your requests miss; with ten servers about nine in ten do. Adding servers made the site worse, which is the opposite of what scaling should do.
steps.idea: When state is kept per server, more servers means more requests reaching a server that does not know the user.
steps.caption: Server B has no record of sid=9f2 and rejects the request.

steps.title: Sticky sessions: a patch
steps.body: A common patch is sticky sessions: the load balancer remembers that sid=9f2 belongs to A (using a cookie or a hash of the client IP) and always sends you there. That works, but it has costs. Load can become uneven when heavy users pile onto one server. Deploys must drain each server slowly. And if A crashes, as shown, every user pinned to A loses their session, because A held the only copy.
steps.idea: Sticky sessions hide the problem but keep it: the server still holds the only copy, so if it dies the data is lost.
steps.caption: Pinned to A, requests work, until A crashes and its sessions disappear.

steps.title: Move sessions to a shared store
steps.body: The real fix is to take the session out of the server. Any app server writes it to a fast shared store such as Redis or Memcached, filed under the session ID. In the animation A (running again after its crash) saves the session there with an expiry of 30 minutes since last use. Because every server talks to the same store, no server holds anything the others lack.
steps.idea: Move the state out: servers keep the logic, and a shared store keeps the memory.
steps.caption: A writes the session to the shared store at login.

steps.title: Any server can answer
steps.body: Now your next click can land on B. B reads the cookie, fetches sess:9f2 from the store (about 1 ms on the same network), learns it is user 42, then asks the database for the cart and returns it. The load balancer can use plain round robin with no pinning. The price is one extra network hop per request, plus a new component to keep highly available, usually with a replica and automatic failover.
steps.idea: Stateless servers pay one cheap lookup per request, and in return the balancer can pick any server.
steps.caption: B looks up the session in the store, then serves the cart.

steps.title: Signed tokens skip the lookup
steps.body: Another route is to put the session data in the client. After login the server issues a signed token, often a JWT. It holds your user ID and an expiry time, plus a signature made with a key. Any server can check that signature in microseconds, so no store is needed at all. The costs: you cannot easily cancel one token before it expires, so keep tokens short-lived (say 15 minutes) with a refresh mechanism, and never put secrets inside, because anyone can read the contents.
steps.idea: Tokens trade easy revocation for needing no session storage on the server.
steps.caption: B checks the token's signature itself; no session store is read.

steps.title: Kill a server, nobody notices
steps.body: With no state on the servers, they are interchangeable. In the animation A fails its health check (the balancer's regular test request), so the load balancer sends everything to B. B finds your session in the store, so you stay logged in. The same trick lets you deploy by replacing servers one at a time, and autoscale by adding or removing them freely. This is what makes servers disposable, and the next lessons build on it.
steps.idea: Stateless servers can be added, removed or killed at any time with no user impact.
steps.caption: A fails its health check; B serves the cart and the session survives.

steps.title: Keep state out of the servers
steps.body: State kept in a server's memory ties users to that server and is lost when it dies. Sticky sessions fix the routing but not the loss. A shared session store or signed tokens move the state out, so any server can answer any request. The state did not vanish: it now lives in a store you must keep fast and durable. Stateless means the app servers are disposable, not that the system has no data.
steps.idea: Stateless app servers scale and fail over easily; the state moves to a few well-protected places.
steps.caption: Servers hold logic only; sessions and data live in shared stores.

quiz.q: You run 5 stateful servers with in-memory sessions and plain round robin. Roughly what share of a logged-in user's requests land on a server that does not know them?
quiz.why: Only the server that handled the login has the session. Each later request picks one of 5 servers evenly, so 4 in 5 (80%) miss.

quiz.q: A team adds sticky sessions and calls the problem solved. Which failure still loses users' logins?
options: A user opens the site in a second tab
The load balancer adds a sixth server
The server holding a user's session crashes
quiz.why: Stickiness only controls routing. The session still exists in one server's memory, so if that server dies or is replaced the session is gone.

quiz.q: Which statement about signed tokens (JWTs) versus a shared session store is correct?
options: Tokens avoid a per-request lookup but are harder to revoke before expiry
Tokens are always more secure because the client holds them
A session store requires sticky sessions to work
Tokens let the server change a user's data without the client noticing
quiz.why: A signed token is verified locally with no store read, but the server holds no record to delete, so early revocation needs extra machinery such as short lifetimes or a deny list.

quiz.q: After moving sessions to Redis, the app servers are stateless. What new risk have you taken on?
options: Servers can no longer be restarted
The session store is now a shared dependency that must be fast and highly available
quiz.why: State did not disappear, it moved. If the session store is down or slow, every server is affected, so it needs replication, failover, and monitoring.

cheatsheet.def: Keeps data between requests (such as a session in RAM) that other servers lack, so requests must reach that same server.
Holds nothing a later request depends on; everything needed arrives with the request or comes from a shared store.
Load balancer pins a user to one server via cookie or IP hash. Easy, but skews load, slows deploys, and loses sessions on a crash.
Redis or Memcached keyed by session ID with a TTL. Costs about 1 ms per request and must be replicated for availability.
Client-held claims signed with a key. No lookup needed, but hard to revoke, so use short expiry plus refresh tokens.
The payoff of statelessness: autoscale, rolling deploys, and failover all work by freely adding or removing app servers.
